"Edges," Penhale says. "Aye. A master doesn't hit the middle of a channel." He puts the tiller over.

It is the strangest twelve minutes of sailing you are ever likely to see. The cutter goes crabwise from one side of the lane to the other, three strokes of the sweeps at a time, while Tam casts and calls and casts again and the notebook fills. The deep water has a floor as flat as a table, six and seven fathoms from side to side. Then, within two boat's lengths, it climbs.

"Six! ... Five! ... By the mark, three! ... Two!"

"Out," says Penhale, and Hob backs her off, and they find the other wall the same way. The southern edge is steep, almost a step. The northern one shelves more gently and is all coarse sand, which comes up yellow in the tallow. Between them you count the cutter's lengths, twice, and both times it comes to a little over two hundred feet.

On the third crossing the lead line trembles in Tam's hand before it has touched anything. A long smooth wrinkle is travelling down the lane toward you from seaward, hardly a ripple. Penhale sees it and his head comes up like a dog's.

"That's the flood. That's our twenty minutes." He does not raise his voice. "Lead aboard, Tam. Hob, both sweeps, and pull as if your mother were watching. Surveyor, put that book inside your coat and take hold of something. We go out the way we came in, and we go now."
I button the notebook inside my coat, take a turn of the mainsheet round my wrist, and keep my eyes on the tower and the beacon. "They're still in line. You're straight."

"Keep telling me," Penhale says through his teeth. "I can't look at them and her both."

The wrinkle becomes a current, and the current becomes a slope. The cutter is being pushed back into the estuary as fast as Hob can pull her out; the two shoulders of surf, which a minute ago stood still, are sliding past the wrong way. Hob's breath comes in sobs. Tam has thrown himself on the loom of the second sweep beside him, his feet off the deck at every stroke.

The tower drifts off the beacon by the width of a finger. You say so, and the tiller moves, and they close again. Twice more it happens. Each time the surf on that side seems to lean toward the boat.

Then the bow lifts to a proper swell, a long green one with weight in it, and the noise falls away astern. The lead-coloured water of the Outer Road opens round you. Hob lets go of his sweep and lies down on the deck exactly where he is.

Penhale brings her head to wind and lets her lie. For a while he only looks back at the bar. The sun is coming up behind the town, and with the tide making, the dark lane is already harder to see; in half an hour there will be nothing there but grey water.

"Twenty-two years," he says. "I've sailed past that twice a day." He turns to you. His voice is rough. "Well. Read it to me. All of it, in order. I want to hear what we did."

I open the notebook and read the casts back in order: the nine in the Outer Road, the run in, the sevens, the three crossings with the edges at two fathoms, and the width I counted. "Thirty-one casts. One tide. It needs checking at high water and along its length before anyone prints it."

Penhale listens to the whole list with his eyes shut. Tam's lips move along with you; he is checking the figures against his own memory and finding them right. When you reach the end there is a silence, with the cutter rocking gently and the gulls beginning.

"Thirty-one casts and no lies in them," Penhale says. "I've known Guild pilots forty years at sea who couldn't bring me that." He opens his eyes. "You want it at high water, and along the length. That's this evening's slack for the one and tomorrow's dawn for the other. Then the springs, when the stream runs hardest, and we see whether she holds her shape."

Hob has sat up. He is rubbing his forearms and looking at the notebook in your hands with something close to awe.

"Seven fathom," he says. "A ship of three hundred tons draws fifteen foot. You could bring the whole fishing fleet through there abreast."

"You could not, and you'll say nothing of the kind ashore." Penhale rounds on him, though without much force. "Not seven, not a channel, not a word. If the Anchor hears there's a way through before the surveyor has laid it down properly, some fool will try it on the ebb by Friday and we'll be fishing him out." He looks at each of them in turn, the boy last. "We went out to prove a new line in the Outer Road. Nine fathoms, sand and shell. That's all we did."

He lays the tiller over for the harbour, and adds to you, lower, "Dallow must be told at once, and nobody else. Will you go to him yourself, or shall I?"
"Together. He'll want to hear it from the skipper who swore it couldn't be done." I wrap the lead back in its sacking. "And I want this line locked up between tides. Where is it safest?"

A sound comes out of Penhale that it takes you a moment to recognise as a laugh.

"Together, then. He'll enjoy that. I've been telling him he was a dreamer since before Tam was born." He steers for the pier head. "As to the line. Aboard, there's the cuddy forward, which has a hasp and a padlock, and I hold the key. Ashore there's Sabel's, with a bolt, and the Guild strongroom, with two locks. A sounding line's no use to a thief. But a line that's a hand short in the fathom is a great deal of use to a man who wants your depths to look wrong."

He lets that sit. The cutter slips in past the pier, where the first fishing boats are putting out, and their crews look across curiously at the Kittiwake coming home at sunrise with her sweeps still wet.

"I'd take it ashore with you," he goes on. "Every time. And I'd measure it against Sabel's studs before each tide, in front of a witness, and have the witness sign your book. Then when Dunmore's people stand up and say the surveyor's line was stretched, you'll have a page to show them." He glances at you sideways. "That's how he'll come at it. He won't say there's no channel. He'll say it can't be trusted."

The quay is close. Nell Harrow is standing on it in her shawl, hugging her elbows, and when she sees the four of you she starts to run along the wall toward the steps. Tam is already waving both arms at her, grinning like a lantern, having evidently forgotten everything his uncle said two minutes ago.

I catch Tam's arm before we reach the steps. "Nine fathoms, sand and shell, Tam. That's what you're pleased about." Then, to Nell, quietly: "We need the master, a closed door, and you to witness a measurement."

Tam's arms drop. He composes his face into an expression of such heavy innocence that Hob has to look away.

Nell reads the four of you in one glance and asks nothing on the quay. Within a quarter of an hour you are in a small panelled room above the chart hall, with the door shut and Dallow standing with his back to the window. Penhale gives the account himself, in his own order: the nine, the run in, the seven. He says the number without expression. Then he says it again.

Dallow sits down rather suddenly on the window seat.

"Seven fathoms. Rock bottom, scoured. Two hundred feet from edge to edge." He passes a hand over his face. "Jory, if this is some slow joke of yours, I'll have your certificate."

"I've not the wit for jokes. Ask her for the book."

The master reads your thirty-one casts through twice. Then he does a thing you had not expected: he calls Nell to the table and has her copy the whole page into the Guild's own sounding ledger, with the date, the state of the tide, and the names of all four who were aboard, and he signs beneath it.

"Now it exists in two places," he says. "Whatever happens to your coat." He looks up. "You said a witness to a measurement. Sabel's studs, I take it, before the evening tide. I'll come myself. And between now and then, surveyor, where does that line sleep?"
"With me, from now on. This morning it was in my hands the whole time. I'll measure it in the yard at four with you watching, and we sail on the evening slack."

So it is arranged, and for most of the day it goes as arranged. You sleep for three hours in the back room with the coiled line under the bed and the bolt shot. At noon the Kittiwake's people eat at the widow's table, since Penhale will not have the Anchor's ears near them, and you carry the line down with you and hang it on the peg by the yard door where you can see it from your chair.

At four Dallow comes through the shop, ducking under the lanterns, with Nell behind him carrying the ledger. Widow Sabel leaves her counter to watch. You lay the first fathom between the brass studs, as you did yesterday.

It does not reach.

The two-tailed leather, which yesterday sat exactly over the second stud at the end of the second fathom, now falls short of it by the length of your hand. You try the next. The three-tailed mark is short by more. By the white rag at five fathoms the error has grown to nearly two feet, and by seven it is a full yard.

Nobody speaks. The widow bends, with a click of her knees, and takes the two-fathom mark between finger and thumb. She turns it over.

"That's not my hitch," she says quietly. "That's a seaman's hitch, and a hasty one. Somebody has had every one of these out and put it back a little nearer the lead." She looks up at you over her spectacles. "This line was right at dawn. You proved it at nine fathoms. When was it out of your sight?"

I go back over the day aloud. "Under my bed, bolted in. Then on that peg through the meal, in front of all of us." I stop. "No. Before the meal I left it in the cuddy for half an hour, padlocked, while I washed. Penhale has the only key."

"I have the only key," Penhale says. He has gone grey under the weather in his face. "And it's on my belt, and has been. But a hasp is held by four screws, and the cuddy's old."

He does not wait. The whole party follows him along the quay to the Kittiwake, the master of the Guild walking with his hands behind him like a mourner. Penhale drops into the cutter, crouches at the little forward door, and puts his thumbnail to the hasp. One of the four screws turns under it without resistance. The slot is bright, and there are fresh splinters in the paint.

"Drawn and put back," he says. "With a knife point, by the look. It would take a man who knew the boat perhaps a quarter of an hour to draw them, shift fifteen marks, and screw her up again." He stays crouched, looking at nothing. "And at that hour there were three of us ashore at Sabel's pump, washing. And one who said he'd stop aboard and grease the thole pins."

Tam makes a small noise.

Dallow lets out his breath. "Where is Hob now?"

"Sent him for tallow," says Penhale. "A quarter hour since. He was very willing to go."

Widow Sabel has followed as far as the quay edge, and stands with her arms folded in her shawl. "He came to me for tallow," she says. "He paid with a new shilling. I wondered at it. Hob never has a shilling before Saturday."

Penhale climbs out of the cutter. His voice is very level. "He'll be at his mother's or at the ropewalk gate. I can have him here in ten minutes. Or you can leave him be and let them think it's worked. It's your line he spoiled, surveyor. Say which."
"Bring him, but gently, and here on the boat, not in the street. I want to know what he was paid to do and what he told them. I'm not interested in seeing him hanged for a shilling."

Penhale goes, with Tam at his heels, and returns in less than the ten minutes. Hob walks between them like a man going to have a tooth drawn. He has plainly been crying, and he begins to speak before anyone has asked him anything.

"I never meant harm to the boat. I'd not harm the boat." He looks at Dallow, at the widow, anywhere but at you. "It was the gentleman in the grey coat. He was at the ropewalk gate last night. He said the Guild was being made a fool of by a stranger with a stretched line, and that it'd be a kindness to the pilots to show it. He said nobody would be hurt. He said if the marks were a bit out, the master would see the figures didn't agree and send her away, and that'd be an end of it, and no one would take a ship in there and drown."

"And he gave you?" says Dallow.

"A pound, sir. In shillings." Hob swallows. "And another pound to say when we sailed and what we found."

The silence that follows is a particular one. Penhale closes his eyes.

"And what did you tell him we found, Hob?" you hear the master ask, very gently.

"Seven fathom." It is hardly audible. "This forenoon, when I went for the grease. I'm sorry, miss. He already knew there was something. He only wanted the number." Hob looks at you at last, wretched and young. "I didn't know then what it meant. I do now. I've been sick about it since dinner."
"Then you can start mending it. Did you move every mark by the same amount, or more as you went up the line? And is the pound still in your pocket?"

Hob blinks. Whatever he was braced for, it was not arithmetic.

"More as I went, miss. He showed me on a bit of string. A thumb at the first mark, two thumbs at the next, and so on up, so it'd look as if the line had stretched the wrong way. He said a stretched line reads deep, and a shrunk one reads shoal, and he wanted it to read shoal." He digs in his breeches and holds out a fist of silver. "Nineteen shillings. I spent the one on tallow."

"On my tallow," says Widow Sabel. "With his money. I'll keep that shilling in a jar."

Dallow has been listening with his head down. Now he raises it, and there is a thoughtful look on the broad creased face that you have not seen there before.

"So Mr Fitch has shown us his hand, and told us what he wants: depths that read shoal and a surveyor who looks careless. And he believes, at this moment, that this evening's soundings will be taken with a false line." He turns to you. "That is worth something. I don't yet know what. You could re-mark the line against the studs in an hour, with all of us to witness it, and sound tonight as planned. Or you might see some use in letting Dunmore think his pound was well spent, for a day."

Penhale says, "I don't like tricks."

"No," Dallow agrees. "You never have. It's the surveyor's line, Jory, and the surveyor's name they'll try to blacken. Let her say."

"No tricks with the depths. I re-mark it now, in front of all of you, and Nell writes down both what was done to it and how it was corrected. Hob signs that page. If Dunmore wants to believe his pound was well spent, let Hob keep the other nineteen shillings and say nothing either way."

"That I can stomach," says Penhale.

It takes the hour Dallow predicted. You carry the line back to the yard and lay it out between the studs, fathom by fathom, and at each mark the widow picks out the seaman's hitch with a marlinspike and ties her husband's knot in its place. Nell kneels on the flags with the ledger on an upturned bucket and writes it as it happens: the error found at each mark, in inches; the correction; the hour. Dallow reads each line over her shoulder.

When the ten-fathom leather is home, Nell turns the ledger and holds out the pen to Hob.

He can write his name and not much more. He does it slowly, pressing hard, under a paragraph that says in plain words what he did, who paid him, and how much. Then he stands holding the pen as if he does not know where to put it.

"That's a brave thing to sign," Dallow tells him. "It's also the only thing that will keep you your berth, so don't think too well of yourself." He takes the ledger and closes it. "This goes in the strongroom beside the chart. Two keys."

The light in the yard has turned yellow. From the quay comes the creak of the Kittiwake's mooring lines as the tide lifts her; high water is close.

Penhale looks at Hob, and then at you. "I sail with three or I sail with four. I can pull a sweep myself. He's been a fool, and he's told the truth after. Do you want him in the boat tonight, or on the quay?"
"In the boat. I'd rather have him where his skipper can see him, and he pulls a better sweep than I do. But Tam carries the line from this yard to the bow, and it doesn't leave his hands or mine."

"You hear that," Penhale says to Hob. "Don't thank her. Pull."

Tam takes the coiled line across his body like a bandolier and will not put it down even to climb aboard.

The evening sounding is a different thing from the dawn. At high water there is no bar to see: only a long uneasy stretch of sea, a shade paler than the rest, with the swell running over it unbroken. Without the tower and the beacon nobody could say where the lane lay. Penhale brings them into line and takes the cutter in under her jib, slowly, into water that looks like any other.

Tam's voice comes back steady this time. "By the mark, ten! ... And a half, ten! ... Ten again!"

Seven fathoms at low water, and the tide here rises twenty feet. The arithmetic is exact. You write it down, with the hour, and something in your chest that has been clenched since four o'clock lets go. The edges are where they were this morning: the steep one to the south, the shelving one to the north, both under more than five fathoms of water now and harmless to anything afloat.

"She holds her shape," Penhale says. It is nearly a prayer.

Coming home in the dusk, Hob speaks for the first time since the quay, without turning his head from his sweep.

"Miss. There's a thing I didn't say before the master. The gentleman asked me one more question, and I'd no answer for him, so I let it go by. He wanted to know what you were called. He said Mr Dunmore couldn't have a paper drawn against a person with no name." He pulls two strokes. "What paper would that be?"

"A writ, I expect. The reward notice said 'instruments unlawfully removed.' He means to use the harbour court." I look at Penhale. "Can a magistrate have something drawn against 'the Guild's surveyor' without a name on it?"

"He can try," says Penhale. "I've seen a writ served on 'the master of the brig lying at the east quay' when nobody could spell the Dutchman's name. It held. The bench took the view that a man doesn't escape the law by being hard to pronounce."

He steers a while in silence. The harbour lights are coming up, yellow in the blue dusk, and the tall house with the green shutters above the fish market has every window lit.

"Instruments unlawfully removed," he says. "That's a claim that something you carry is his. He'll not mean the line, you bought that from Sabel and half the quay saw it. He'll mean what you brought with you. What's in your satchel, and that brass tube, and anything else a surveyor walks about with." He glances at you. "If the bench finds for him, even for a week while it's argued, the bailiff takes the lot into keeping. Your notebook's an instrument, to a lawyer. So is a chart."

Tam has turned round on his thwart. "The chart's in the strongroom. With two keys."

"A bailiff with a warrant doesn't need keys, boy. He needs Dallow to choose between opening the door and being fined for contempt." Penhale brings the cutter round the pier head. "I'm a pilot and not an attorney. But I'd say that dinner he asked you to wasn't an idle courtesy. A man who can have a writ drawn tomorrow doesn't feed you tonight unless he'd sooner not use it."

On the Guild quay a figure is waiting under the lamp, with a paper in his gloved hand. It is not Nell this time. The coat is grey.
I step up onto the quay and stop in front of him, leaving the line with Tam in the boat. "Mr Fitch. If that paper is a writ, you'll want to serve it in front of witnesses. You have three."

Fitch takes off his hat. Under the lamp he looks older than he did at Thornby, and rather tired; there is harbour mud on his good boots.

"It is nothing so disagreeable, madam. It is a card." He holds it out between two gloved fingers. It is a square of stiff paper with four lines of copperplate: Mr Dunmore's compliments, and the pleasure of the surveyor's company at dinner, this evening, at eight. There is no name on it but his. "My employer observes that you were unable to come last night, and supposes that you were occupied. He thought the hour of high water might find you at liberty."

Behind you, in the cutter, nobody moves. You can feel Penhale not saying anything.

"I am to add three things," Fitch goes on, in the same level voice. "That you may bring whom you please. That nothing will be asked of you at his table except your opinion. And that a certain document, which is drawn and wants only a signature and one particular, will remain in his desk until you have dined, whatever you decide. He gives his word on that, and I have never known him break it." A very faint flush has come into his face. "He also asked me to say that he regrets the business with the sounding line. It was done on my advice and not his, and he thinks it was beneath us. So, for what it is worth, do I."

He puts his hat back on and waits, the card still held out.

I take the card. "Tell him eight o'clock. I'll bring the master of the Guild, if he'll come, and I'll bring nothing else: no notebook, no case." I turn to Penhale. "Will you see the line and my satchel into the strongroom tonight?"

"I'll carry them there myself and stand by while Nell turns her key," Penhale says. He has come up onto the quay with the satchel already in his hand. "And then I'll sit in the Anchor where I can see his front door, and if you're not out of it by midnight, I'll come and knock."

Fitch inclines his head to the three of them, as if this were a perfectly ordinary arrangement, and walks away along the wall.

Dallow, when he is found, hears the invitation without surprise. He changes his coat, grumbling, and at five minutes to eight the two of you climb the lane behind the fish market to the tall house with the green shutters. Widow Sabel has lent you a dark wool gown that belonged to a daughter and brushed your hair herself, with no word spoken about either.

A maid shows you into a room that is all firelight and polished wood. There are charts on the walls here too, old ones, framed, of coasts that have nothing to do with this one. The man standing at the hearth turns as you come in.

He is about fifty, not tall, neatly made, with close-cut grey hair and an indoor pallor that sits oddly on a shipowner. He has a way of looking at a person with his whole attention, as though nobody else had ever been so interesting.

"Osric. It's good of you." And then to you, with a small bow, "And the surveyor, who walked the harbor road in four days with my man two hours behind her the whole way, and whose name I have been unable to buy from anyone between Saltmarsh and here. I'm Dunmore. You'll take a glass of wine before we quarrel?"
"One glass. And I'd rather not quarrel on an empty stomach, so perhaps we could eat while you tell me what you want my opinion on."

"Practical," says Dunmore, and seems genuinely pleased. "Osric, you've engaged a practical woman. I begin to see why I couldn't find her."

The dinner is good and plain: a baked turbot, a dish of leeks, new bread. Dunmore carves the fish himself and gives you the best of it. He eats little. For a quarter of an hour he talks, easily and well, about nothing that matters: the price of hemp, a Dutch chartmaker he once met, the vanity of harbour boards. Dallow answers in grunts. It is like watching a man tune an instrument.

Then he lays down his fork.

"Your opinion, then. Here is the case. A man's father is drowned on that bar when the man is nine years old. He grows up and he spends thirty years, and more money than he will admit to, finding out how to bring a ship across it alive. He does it by losing boats. He does it by paying pilots to go where the Guild forbade them. In the end he has it: eleven marks, known to himself and four men who have eaten his bread for twenty years. With those marks his three cutters bring in forty ships a season, and none of them has touched." He turns his wineglass by the stem. "And then the Guild hires a stranger, who climbs a lighthouse, and in one tide proposes to hand what cost him thirty years to any master with a shilling. I should like to know, surveyor, whether you think that just."

"I think thirty years of work deserves to be paid for. I don't think it deserves to be owned. Eleven men died on the Wren two winters ago with your marks sitting in your desk. Did you know about the gap, Mr Dunmore?"

The fire ticks. Dallow has stopped chewing.

Dunmore does not look away, and he does not answer quickly. When he does, the easy voice has gone out of him and something plainer has come in.

"I knew there was deep water somewhere north of where my marks take a ship. I did not know where to within a quarter mile, and I did not know its width. My way in is a dog-leg over the southern tail of the bar, with nine feet at half tide. It is slow, and it wants a pilot who has done it fifty times, and that is exactly why it was worth having." He sets the glass down. "The Wren's master was offered one of my pilots off the Point, at my usual rate. He refused. He said he'd come in on Guild marks or none. I have asked myself since whether my rate was what killed him. I've not found an answer I can sleep on. That is the truth, and Osric knows it, because I told him the week we buried them."

"He did," says Dallow, into his plate. "I'll give him that."

"So." Dunmore draws a breath, and the attention comes back into his face like a lamp being turned up. "You've found in a day what I could not find in thirty years, and by now you've sounded it. Seven fathoms, I'm told. I won't insult you by pretending I don't know. Here is what I propose instead of a quarrel, and I'd ask you to hear all of it before you say no."
"I'm listening. All of it."

He counts the points on the tablecloth with one forefinger.

"First. Two hundred pounds, paid tomorrow, for an exact copy of your survey. Not the only copy. A copy. The Guild keeps its own.

"Second. The Guild publishes, as it means to. But it publishes in a year, not in a month. For that one year my cutters have the gap to themselves, at a fixed rate that Osric may set and I'll swear to, so that no master is squeezed. I use the year to turn three pilot cutters into something else, since a channel any fool can follow has no need of pilots, and I'd sooner not put forty men on the parish at Christmas.

"Third. The document in my desk is burned in this grate tonight, in front of you both."

He sits back.

"That is the offer. I think it is a fair one, and I think Osric thinks so too, though he'd die sooner than say it at my table." Dallow says nothing at all, which is itself an answer of a kind. "The other road is this. Tomorrow I sign. The writ says that the level, the dividers and the brass case you carry were bought in the south with my advance, by an agent who was mine before he was the Guild's, and who then took a second fee to send you here instead. All of which is true. I have his receipt. The bench impounds your instruments and your papers while it's argued, and the springs come and go."

He spreads his hands, not unkindly.

"I would much rather burn it. But I need one thing to sign it, and I shan't pretend I've stopped looking. What do you say?"

"I say no to the year. A year is another winter, and winter is when the Wren went down. But I'll say this to Osric in front of you: your pilots know that water better than anyone, and a new channel needs buoys, a leading light, and men to keep them. That's work the Guild could pay your forty men to do."

For a moment neither man moves. Then Dallow puts down his knife and looks at you as he looked at the chart on Nell's desk.

"Buoys," he says slowly. "Two, at the edges, and a lit mark on Gull Rock to carry the line at night. Dues on every keel that comes through, a penny a ton, to keep them. The Guild's talked of harbour dues for thirty years and never had anything to charge for." He turns in his chair. "It would want a tender. Three, in time. Black ones with a yellow stripe would do as well as any."

Dunmore has gone very still. He is looking at the fire.

"A keeper of buoys," he says. "At a penny a ton. After thirty years." There is no telling from his voice whether it is the beginning of a laugh or of something else. "You have a hard way of being generous, madam."

He rises, and you and Dallow with him. He goes to a writing desk in the corner, unlocks a drawer and takes out a folded sheet with a ribbon through it. He stands holding it, between the desk and the grate, for what seems a long while.

"No," he says at last, quietly, and lays it back in the drawer. "Not tonight. I gave my word it would stay there until you had dined, and you have. I did not say what I would do after. I must think, and I think badly when I'm beaten at my own table." He turns the key. "I'll tell you honestly how it stands. If I can put a name on that paper by Thursday, I shall sign it, and let three magistrates decide between us. If I cannot, it's waste paper. Is that plain enough to be fair?"

"It's plain. It isn't fair, but I'd rather be told than surprised." I pick up my borrowed shawl. "Thank you for the turbot, Mr Dunmore. I'll be sounding the length of the channel at dawn, if you'd like to watch from your window."

That does draw a laugh from him, short and surprised.

"I shall. With a glass. I've watched that water every morning for thirty years, and I never once thought to look in the right place." He walks you to the door of the room himself. In the hall, with the maid holding your shawl, he says in a lower voice, meant only for you, "For what it's worth, I would have liked to have hired you first. I'd have paid better than the Guild. I'd also have locked up what you found, and you would have despised me for it within the month. So perhaps it's as well."

He bows. The door with the green shutters closes behind you.

The lane is dark and smells of fish and coal smoke. Dallow walks beside you without speaking as far as the corner, his hands behind his back.

"Thursday," he says then. "Three days. He's had every clerk and carrier on the coast asked, and nothing. If nobody's given it to him by now, I don't see who would." He stops under the lamp at the top of the quay steps and looks at you, frowning a little. "Unless there's somebody on that road who has it. I've not asked you, and I'm not asking for the thing itself. But I'd be a poor master if I didn't ask this much. Is there anyone between here and Saltmarsh who could put a name in his hand, if he found them?"

"One person. An innkeeper at the very start of the road, and I'd stake my instruments she'd burn her own taproom before she told him. He's had a man sitting in it for a week, and he still has nothing."

Dallow nods slowly, and some of the weight goes out of his shoulders.

"One. And she's held for a week with his man under her roof." He starts down the steps. "Then I'll sleep. I wasn't sure I would."

Across the quay the door of the Anchor stands open on a bar of yellow light, and in it, on a bench that commands the whole lane, sits Penhale with an untouched pot in front of him. He sees the two of you, lifts three fingers a few inches off the table, and lets them fall. It is probably the warmest greeting he has ever given anyone.

Dallow snorts. "He'd have knocked, too. At midnight, to the minute." At the chandlery door he stops and holds out his hand. "Buoys," he says again, shaking his head, and goes off toward the hall, a heavy, rolling figure, humming something under his breath.

Widow Sabel has left the shop door on the latch and a candle burning on the counter, a white one. Beside it lies a sealed letter, addressed in a cramped clerkly hand to The Surveyor, at the Guild Hall, Greywater, and readdressed in Nell's quick script to the chandlery. It has come by the afternoon carrier. There is a second, smaller packet with it, tied in oilcloth and string, that has plainly travelled much farther and by rougher hands; the knot on it is one you have seen before, on a cloth bundle of bread and cheese.
I open the oilcloth packet first, carefully, by the candle.

The knot comes apart at one pull, the way it was tied to. Inside the oilcloth is a small stone pot sealed with wax, which smells of comfrey when you lift it, and a half sheet of coarse paper folded in four. The writing on it is large, square and unpractised, the hand of someone who keeps accounts and seldom writes anything else. There is no greeting and no signature.

"A carrier I trust is going north so I send this by him. The thin one came back from the road with nothing and sat in my taproom five days. Then a gentleman's clerk came with a purse and asked me straight out what my lodger of that night was called. I told him I keep a house and not a register, and that I have a poor head for names and a worse one for faces. He left the purse on my bar. I sent the girl after him with it. He will not get it here. Change the dressing every evening till the skin is whole and keep it from the salt. The room over the kitchen is still yours."

That is all. At the bottom, as an afterthought, a single line has been squeezed in sideways: "Burn this."

The candle flame leans in a draught from the stairs. Above you a board creaks; Widow Sabel is awake, and tactfully not coming down. The other letter lies where it was, square and neat, with a blob of red wax on the back that has been pressed with something finely engraved: a tiny clock face, the hands at five to twelve.
I hold the half sheet to the candle and let it burn in the widow's ash pan until nothing is left. Then I break the red seal on the second letter.

The coarse paper catches at one corner and is gone in a few breaths, curling black in the pan. You stir the ash with the snuffer until it is powder.

The second letter is three sides of small, dry, exact handwriting, dated from Thornby four days ago.

"Madam. I write because I have been asked about you and think you would wish to know it. The day after the market a gentleman in a grey coat returned to my stall. He was civil. He wished to learn whether I had observed any name or mark upon a pocket compass I had lately reglazed for a traveller, and he offered five guineas for my recollection.

"I told him the truth, which is that a maker of instruments reads a great many inscriptions and that it is the first rule of my trade to forget every one of them before the customer has left the booth. A man who repeated what he read inside watch cases would have no custom in a month. He raised his offer twice. I regret to say I enjoyed refusing it.

"I add, for your use if it should come to a court, that the instrument is Fennick's work and some forty years old; that its glass was cracked through long before this season; and that the inscription within was cut when the brass was new, by the maker's own engraver, as the wear upon it shows. It was therefore never bought with any money advanced this year. I will swear to that before any bench, and enclose a statement signed and witnessed to the same effect.

"The new glass should give no trouble. If it fogs, bring it back. Your obedient servant, Corwin Hale."

The enclosed statement is there, on a separate sheet, with two signatures under his. Footsteps are coming down the stairs after all: the widow, in a shawl and a nightcap, with a second candle.

"I'm not asking what was in them," she says. "I'm asking whether you'll sleep, with three hours to dawn, or sit there. And whether that second one ought to be in a strongbox."

"The second one is evidence, and it goes to Nell at first light. The first one doesn't exist any more." I fold Hale's statement inside my bodice. "Three hours' sleep, then. Wake me at half past three."

She wakes you at half past three, and it feels like ten minutes. The air that comes in when she unbolts the shop is different from yesterday's: soft, damp, and oddly warm, with no stars. The weathercock on the Guild dome, when you pass under it, has swung round into the south-west.

Nell is at the side door of the hall in her shawl, yawning, both keys ready. She takes Hale's statement, reads the first lines by her lantern, and looks up with her eyes very bright. "Forty years old. Oh, I should like to see Mr Fitch's face." It goes into the strongroom drawer beside the chart, and the line and your satchel come out. You measure the first ten fathoms against a brass rule let into the hall's own doorstep, with Nell holding the lantern and writing the hour, and every mark sits where it should.

The Kittiwake is waiting, sweeps out. Penhale glances at the sky and at the weathercock and says nothing about either. Tam takes the line from you with both hands.

Outside the pier the swell has changed too. Yesterday it was short and grey. This morning it comes in long, slow, oily ridges from the south-west, far apart, and the cutter climbs each one and slides down its back with a sickly, sideways motion. On the bar the surf is not tearing any longer. It booms.

"That's weather," Penhale says at last. "A day off, maybe two. The sea always knows before the sky." He brings the tower onto the beacon. "We'll have our slack this morning and it'll be an ugly one. You said the length of it. In at the seaward end, straight through, and out into the estuary. Are you still of that mind?"
"Yes. If the weather's coming, this may be the last quiet slack before the springs. Straight through, one cast every boat's length, and I'll take a bearing on the tower at each one."

"Every boat's length," Penhale says to Tam. "You heard. Don't hurry your cast for anyone, me included."

The lane opens ahead, darker than ever under the low sky. On either hand the swell rears up as it feels the sand, stands for an instant like a wall of bottle glass, and comes down with a concussion you feel in your teeth. In the lane itself the same swell only lifts the cutter, high, and sets her down. It is like walking a plank between two waterfalls.

"By the mark, seven! ... Seven! ... And a half, six! ... Seven!"

Hob pulls like a machine, his eyes fixed on his skipper's face. Nobody has spoken to him this morning beyond orders and he seems grateful for it. You call the tower and the beacon at every cast, write the depth, write the count. Twenty casts. Thirty. The walls of surf begin to fall astern.

"Six! ... By the deep, six! ... Five and a half!"

"She's shoaling," says Penhale sharply.

"Five! ... Five! ... By the mark, five!" Tam plumbs it, and brings the lead up. There is fine grey mud in the tallow, soft as butter. "Mud, Uncle Jory. Five fathom and mud."

Penhale lets out a long breath. The water around the cutter has gone quiet and brown. Ahead lies the whole wide estuary, flat as a pond, with the saltworks chimney standing up on the southern shore and a heron fishing on a mudbank.

"That's the river's own bottom. We're through. We are inside the bar, at dead low water, and we never touched." He looks back along the lane, then at you. "How long was she? You counted."

I add up the column. "Forty-four casts at a boat's length. Thirteen hundred feet, near enough, from the first seven outside to the mud inside. Never less than five fathoms on the line of the tower and the beacon. I want to run it back out to be sure."

"A quarter of a mile," Penhale says. "A quarter of a mile of deep water, and three hundred years of drowned men either side of it." He rubs his face with his maimed hand. "You'll run it back. Of course you will. Tam, change hands on that line before your arm drops off."

There are perhaps six minutes of slack left. He turns the cutter in her own length and takes her back out, a little north of the line this time, at your asking, so that the second run tests the shelving edge. The sevens come again, and the sixes; once, a five and a half with yellow sand, where the northern wall begins to climb, and Penhale edges her south without being told. The figures agree with yesterday's crossings to within half a fathom everywhere. You say so aloud.

"Then it's a channel," he says. "Not a hole. A channel, with a beginning and an end, that you could draw with a ruler."

The first wrinkle of the flood meets you just as the bow lifts to open water, and this time it helps: it has not yet turned in the lane, and the Kittiwake slides out between the booming shoulders as if she had been doing it all her life.

Nobody cheers. Hob ships his sweep and sits with his head on his knees. Tam is coiling the line in long careful loops, and when he reaches the lead he turns it over and looks at the scratch on its foot, and then puts it inside his jersey against his chest.

To the south-west, low down, there is now a bar of cloud the colour of a bruise. Penhale studies it.

"Tomorrow night's high water is the top of the springs," he says. "The one Dallow wants sounded, when the stream runs hardest. And that's coming to meet it. I'll take you if you ask me. But I'll tell you now what I think of it, if you want to hear."
"I do. You've been right about everything except whether it could be done."

One corner of Penhale's mouth moves.

"Then here it is. You have the channel at low water twice and at high water once, and it's the same channel each time. That's a survey. A careful man might ask to see it at the springs, and Dallow is a careful man. But what the springs will tell you is how hard the stream runs through it, and I can tell you that without a lead: hard. Five knots on the ebb, with that width and that depth. A ship must come in on the last of the flood or at slack, and never, never on the ebb. Write that in letters an inch high."

He nods toward the bruise in the sky.

"And that is a south-westerly gale, and it'll be blowing straight onto the bar by tomorrow's dusk, with the biggest tide of the month under it. There will be no slack worth the name. If I take this cutter into the lane in that, to count fathoms, I'm risking four lives to put a number in a book that already has the number in it."

He has said it without heat. He steers for the pier.

"So my advice is, we don't go. You lay down what you have, and you put the note about the stream in the margin on my word and Tane's, and it's an honest chart." He glances at you. "But I said I'd take you if you asked, and I will. I only ask you not to ask because of what a shipowner might say on Thursday."
"I won't ask. Four soundings of the same channel are enough, and your note about the ebb is worth more than a fifth. We stay in harbour tomorrow night, and I spend today laying it down fair."

Penhale looks at you for a moment longer than the remark seems to need. Then he nods once, and some last reserve goes out of the way he stands at the tiller.

"Good. I've sailed with masters who couldn't have said that."

You spend the day as you promised. Nell clears the big table in the upper room and pins down a sheet of the Guild's best paper, and Dallow sends up a steel straightedge six feet long that his predecessor bought and nobody has used since. The dawn sheet comes out of the strongroom, under both keys. By noon the bar is drawn in ink, with Tane's nineteen crosses and the names of the ships beside them. By three the channel lies across it: two fine parallel lines a quarter of a mile long, with the soundings written small between them in fathoms, the nature of the bottom at each, and the two leading marks drawn in elevation at the edge of the sheet, the tower standing above the beacon.

In the margin, in letters not quite an inch high, you write what Penhale told you to.

Nell has hardly spoken for an hour. She has been ruling the border, with her tongue between her teeth, and making a clean copy of the sounding ledger to be bound in with it. Now she straightens up, wipes her pen, and frowns at the bottom corner of the sheet, where there is an empty space.

"It wants a title. And it wants a surveyor." She tilts her head at you. "Every chart in this building says who made it. Master Halloran's, and old Pym's, and the Dutchman's. What's to go there?"

"'A Survey of the Bar and the New Channel at Greywater, from soundings taken aboard the pilot cutter Kittiwake, J. Penhale master, and from the wreck ledger of B. Tane, keeper of the Point light.' Then my two initials and the year. Nothing more."

Nell writes it out on a scrap first, to judge the spacing, and reads it back under her breath. At "J. Penhale master" she smiles. At the end she looks up.

"Two letters. After all that." But she does not argue. She rules three faint pencil lines in the corner and begins to letter the title in a round Italian hand far finer than her everyday one, the tip of her tongue showing. "Jory will pretend he doesn't care that he's on it. And then he'll come in when he thinks I'm at dinner and look at it for a quarter of an hour."

The light from the windows has turned an odd brassy colour. Down on the quays men are doubling mooring lines and carrying sweeps and oars up into the lofts; a string of fishing boats is coming in early, one behind another, under scraps of sail. The weathercock on the dome over your heads gives a long shriek and steadies, pointing dead south-west.

Dallow comes in with rain on his shoulders. He stands in front of the finished sheet for a full minute without a word, and then blows his nose loudly.

"The glass has dropped an inch since noon," he says. "I've had the storm cone hoisted. Every boat that belongs here is in or coming in." He walks to the seaward window and stands with his hands behind him. "Tane has a signal flying at the Point. I can't make it out in this murk, and it's not one of the usual ones. Surveyor, your eyes are thirty years younger than mine. There's a glass on the sill. Tell me what he's showing."
I take the telescope from the sill, steady it against the window frame, and find the Point. "Two flags, one above the other, and a black ball under them. What does that mean?"

In the round of the glass the lighthouse stands out pale against a sky like wet slate. The lamp is already lit, hours early. From the gallery rail two flags are streaming out stiff as boards, and beneath them a dark shape swings on a halyard.

"Describe the flags," says Dallow, without turning round.

The upper one is red with a white square. The lower is plain yellow. You tell him so, and hear Nell's pen stop.

"Vessel in the offing, standing in." Dallow's voice has gone very quiet. "And the ball is 'in difficulty.' He's not flown that since the Wren." He takes the telescope from you, wipes the eyepiece on his cuff and looks for himself, and then swings it slowly to the left, out over the grey heaving water beyond the bar. He holds it there a long time.

"There. Brig. Under topsails and a rag of jib, and she's lost her fore-topmast, it's hanging in the rigging." He hands the glass back so that you can see. She is perhaps four miles off, a small dark shape that leans and recovers and leans again, with something trailing at her bow like a broken wing. "She can't claw off with that forward. She's in the bay with the wind dead onshore and the whole bar under her lee. She'll have seen the town and be running for it, because there's nowhere else."

Feet are pounding on the stairs. Penhale comes in without knocking, oilskins streaming, Tam behind him.

"You've seen her," he says. "The Calloway, out of Marrow, in timber. I know her topsails. Eleven hands and the master's wife." He looks at Dallow, and then, deliberately, at you. "She'll be on the bar in two hours. High water's at ten past eight."

"Then she arrives near the top of the flood, with twenty feet over the channel and the stream still running in, not out." I put my finger on the chart at the seaward end. "If someone can put her on the line of the tower and the beacon, she'll come through. Can a brig with no fore-topmast hold a straight course for a quarter of a mile?"

"Before the wind, yes," says Penhale. "It's all she can do. Running straight is the one thing left to her." He comes to the table and leans over the sheet, dripping on Nell's border, and nobody stops him. His three fingers trace the two fine lines. "On the flood, with ten fathoms in the lane. God. It's as if it were made for it."

"It was drawn this afternoon," Dallow says heavily. "The ink's wet. No master alive has seen it but the people in this room."

"Then somebody must take it to him." Penhale straightens. "He can't see the leading marks from out there in this. The beacon's a stick in the spray, and by half past seven it'll be dark. He'll steer for the harbour lights, which is what the Wren did, and they'll lead him onto the tail of the bar a half mile south."

Nobody says anything. The rain comes against the window in a single sheet.

"The Kittiwake can live out there for an hour," Penhale goes on, in the flat voice he used in the Anchor to explain why a thing could not be done. "No longer. Long enough to get to windward of the lane, show a light, and lead him in. But I can't lead and take marks both, not in the dark. I need someone in the bow who knows where the edges are without seeing them. Who has them in her head, to the fathom." He does not look at Tam. "There's one person in Greywater who's been across that lane five times with a pencil in her hand. I'll not order it. It isn't Guild work, and you're not Guild."

"I'm coming. I'll need the lead line, a dark lantern, and the telescope. And we need a light on Gull Rock to stand for the beacon, and one in the church tower above it. Who can do that inside an hour?"

"Pask," say Dallow and Nell together.

Nell is already at the door. "He's keys to the tower, and he'd climb it in a hurricane to spite the curate. I'll tell him every lantern in the vestry." She is gone, her feet rattling down the stairs.

"Gull Rock," Dallow says. "That's a boat, and a landing on wet weed in a gale, and a man to stand there holding a flare for an hour with the sea coming over him." He rubs his jaw. "I've pilots who could. Whether I've pilots who will, for a channel they've been told all their lives isn't there..."

He is interrupted. The door, which Nell left swinging, opens again, and Mr Fitch stands in it with his hat in his hand and water running off the skirts of the grey coat. He is out of breath. He has evidently run up from the quay.

"Master Dallow. Madam." He bows, absurdly, to each. "Mr Dunmore's compliments. He has been watching the brig from his window this half hour. He asks me to say that his three cutters are manned and at the east quay, with their best men, and that they are at the Guild's orders for tonight. He names no terms." Fitch draws a breath. "He also says that he supposes somebody will want a light shown on the Rock, and that he would be obliged if he might be the one to hold it. He knows the landing. He has known it since he was nine."

"Tell him yes, and tell him the light must show from the Rock by half past seven and not go out, whatever comes over him. The tower will be lit above it. When the two are in line, that's the channel." I pick up the coiled line. "And Mr Fitch, thank him."

"I will tell him exactly that," says Fitch, and for an instant something that is not a servant's expression crosses his face. Then he is gone, as quickly as Nell.

After that the evening comes apart into pieces, each sharp and separate. The quay in the half dark, lanterns swinging, men running with coils of rope. Widow Sabel on her doorstep in the rain, pushing a tin of tallow and a flask into your pockets without a word. The three black cutters with the yellow stripe casting off from the east quay one after another; in the stern of the first a slight, bareheaded figure sits with a great iron cresset between his knees, and does not look round.

The Kittiwake goes out under a scrap of reefed mainsail, and the sea beyond the pier head is like nothing you have seen from her deck before. The long oily ridges have become hills. She climbs each one at a slant and falls off its crest with a crash that shakes the mast, and the spray comes aft in solid lumps. Hob is lashed to the pump. Tam is lashed to the mast with the line across his chest. Penhale has taken a turn of rope round his own waist and the tiller both.

"There's the tower!" he shouts.

High over the dark town a cluster of yellow sparks has appeared, crowded together: every lantern in the vestry. A minute later, low on the water to seaward, a second light flares up red and smoky, dips as a sea breaks across it, and burns again.

Out in the blackness beyond the bar, a third light answers: a ship's lantern, swinging wildly, coming in fast.

I wedge myself in the bow with the dark lantern and the telescope. "Put us at the seaward end of the lane and hold us there. When she's close enough I'll show the light and call the marks back to you. Tam, sound when I say, not before."

"Seaward end," Penhale shouts back. "Tell me when the lights come on!"

The yellow cluster and the red flare are still far apart, the one high and to the right, the other low and to the left. As the cutter claws south they begin to close. It is slow work and every sea tries to undo it. Twice the red light vanishes altogether for the space of several breaths, and you find you are counting, and each time it climbs back up out of the dark.

Then the yellow stands directly over the red.

"On!" The word is torn out of your mouth by the wind, and you scream it again. Penhale heaves on the tiller. The Kittiwake comes round onto the line, bow to the town, and at once the motion changes. To the left and the right, close, the hills of water are rearing up white and falling over with a noise like cannon. Here they only lift her.

"Sound!"

Tam's arm swings. "No bottom at ten!" It is a thin high yell. "No bottom!"

"We're in the mouth of it," Penhale bawls. "Now where's that brig?"

She is very near. You can see her without the glass: a black mass, enormous after the cutter, with a white bone of foam under her forefoot and the wreck of her topmast thrashing alongside. She is coming straight down wind, as he said she would. And she is not on the line. She is steering for the harbour lights, a long way south of the yellow sparks, and on that course she will pass the Kittiwake a hundred yards to the left and go on into the breakers.

There is a speaking trumpet in the rack by your knee. There is the dark lantern in your hand, with its shutter.

I open the lantern's shutter full toward the brig and swing it in a wide arc from her bow toward our stern, again and again, then put the trumpet to my mouth. "Calloway! Follow my light! Tower over the red flare! Deep water! Follow me in!"

The wind takes most of it. You swing the lantern until your shoulder burns, the same arc each time: from her, to you, to the lights beyond.

For what feels like a long while nothing changes. The brig comes on, huge and blind. You can see men on her forecastle now, small pale faces, one of them pointing at the cutter. A voice comes down the wind, a single hoarse word that might be "Where?"

"Tower over the flare!" Tam has added his voice to yours without leaving his line, and it carries better, high and piercing. "In line! In line! Seven fathom!"

On the brig's quarterdeck somebody moves. A lantern is lifted and swung once, twice, in answer. Then, with dreadful slowness, the bone of foam under her bow begins to shift. Her bowsprit swings across the harbour lights, across the dark gap between, and steadies, pointing over the Kittiwake's mast at the cluster of yellow sparks on the hill.

"He's seen it!" Penhale's voice cracks. "He's coming onto the line. Now lead him, for God's sake, he'll be up our stern in a minute!"

The cutter gathers way before the wind, into the lane. On both hands the breakers stand up higher than her mast. Behind her, filling the whole sky, comes the brig.

"Sound!"

"By the mark, ten! ... Ten! ... And a half, nine!"

The red flare is close ahead and to the left, on its rock, streaming flat in the gale. A figure is crouched behind it, holding the iron basket up with both arms. As you watch, a sea breaks clean over the rock and light and man disappear together.

"Hold the line, Jory, steer on the tower alone! It's dead ahead, you don't need the flare for the next hundred yards!" I keep the lantern trained aft on the brig and count the seconds until the red light comes back.

"On the tower!" Penhale answers, and the cutter does not waver.

You count. Five. Ten. The rock is a heap of white water. Behind you the brig's lantern swings on, steady, trusting the small light ahead of her.

Fifteen. A spark. It wavers, gutters, and then climbs: the cresset, lifted again above the foam at the full stretch of a man's arms, flaring up red as he feeds it. You can see him now, hatless and streaming, on his knees on the weed with a second figure in a pale coat holding him by the belt.

"He's there!" yells Tam. "He's there, he never let go of it!"

"Sound, boy!"

"Nine! ... Ten! ... By the deep, nine!"

The walls of surf slide past. They are thunderous and very close, and neither of them touches her. You call the marks back between Tam's casts: the steep edge to the south, forty yards; the shelving edge to the north, more. Penhale steers down the middle as if it were a street.

Then the noise begins to drop astern. The cutter's motion eases, shortens, and flattens out.

"Seven! ... Six! ... By the mark, five!" Tam hauls in. His voice breaks into a sob of laughter. "Mud! Mud, Uncle Jory!"

Penhale puts the helm down and the Kittiwake rounds up, shaking, into quiet brown water. Out of the smother behind her, between the two walls of the bar, the Calloway comes through: slowly, hugely, with her broken topmast dragging and every soul aboard her crowded along the rail. She passes within a boat's length. On her quarterdeck a man in a sou'wester has taken off his hat, in the rain, and is holding it against his chest.
I close the lantern's shutter and sit down on the wet deck where I am, because my legs won't hold me. "Count them, Tam. Count the people on her rail."

Tam climbs as high in the shrouds as his lashing allows and counts aloud, pointing, as the brig drifts past and begins to let go her anchor.

"...nine, ten, eleven. And a lady, by the wheel, in a man's coat. That's twelve." He turns round, his face shining wet in the glow of the binnacle. "Twelve, miss. That's all of them. That's every one."

Hob has stopped pumping and is crying openly, with his mouth open, like a child. Penhale stands at the tiller with the rope still round his waist and looks at the brig's riding light as it steadies and holds. He says something that the wind does not carry. Then, louder, without turning his head:

"Eleven men. Two winters ago, half a mile from here." He wipes his face with the back of his maimed hand. "Tonight, twelve, and a broken spar."

From the town, faint against the gale, a bell has begun to ring: not a tolling, but a fast, wild, uneven clanging, as if the ringer were laughing while he pulled. It goes on and on.

"That's Pask," says Tam. "That's the Guild bell. He only rings her for a ship saved."

Astern, the red light on Gull Rock is still burning. A black cutter with a yellow stripe is working up under its lee, pitching heavily, to take two men off.

Penhale unties the rope from his waist. "They'll want you on the quay," he says to you. "The whole town will be there. The brig's master will want to know who showed him that lantern, and he'll ask for a name to thank." He looks down at you, sitting in the scuppers with the dark lantern in your lap. "What do I tell him?"

"Tell him it was the Kittiwake, and that the channel's on a chart at the Guild hall, where he can buy a copy next month like everyone else." I get to my feet, holding the shrouds. "And take us in by the Guild steps, not the main quay. I want to see Dunmore brought ashore."

"The Kittiwake," Penhale repeats. "Aye. That'll do very well." He brings her head round for the harbour.

The main quay is black with people and bright with torches, and the roar that goes up as the cutter passes the pier head reaches you even across the wind. Penhale keeps to the far side, in the dark, and slides her in to the weedy steps under the Guild hall where only two figures are waiting: Dallow, bareheaded in the rain, and Nell with a blanket over her arm.

The black cutter comes in a few minutes later, to the same steps, as if by agreement. Four of her people lift a man out of the stern sheets. He is wrapped in a boat cloak and he cannot stand without help; his hands, when the lantern catches them, are raw and blistered across both palms where the iron of the cresset has burned through his gloves. Fitch climbs out after him, his grey coat torn from collar to hem, and takes his arm.

Dunmore looks up the steps and sees who is standing there. He stops. Water runs out of his hair into his eyes.

"Twelve, they tell me," he says. His voice is nearly gone. "Is that right?"

"Twelve," says Dallow.

Dunmore nods. He looks at you for a moment, with that whole attention of his, and then down at his own ruined hands, held out a little in front of him as though they belonged to someone else.

"It went out once," he says. "For a quarter of a minute. I thought I'd drowned them." He draws a long, unsteady breath. "Mr Fitch. In the top drawer of my desk there is a paper with a ribbon through it. Be so good as to go up to the house, now, and fetch it down here." He raises his eyes to yours again. "Unless the surveyor would sooner I burned it in my own grate, where she can't see it done."
"Here, please. On the steps, with the four of us to see it. Then go home and have those hands dressed. Honey and yarrow, if your housekeeper has them; I can recommend it."

Something that is almost a smile crosses the grey, exhausted face.

"Honey and yarrow. I'll tell her it's on a surveyor's authority."

Fitch is gone and back in ten minutes, running in his torn coat. The paper he brings has a green ribbon through one corner and is covered on both sides in a lawyer's close script. Near the top of the first page, in the middle of a line, there is a gap the length of a finger, left blank.

Dunmore cannot hold it. He nods to Fitch, who offers it first to you, so that you may see what it is, and then holds one corner in the flame of Nell's lantern. It burns slowly, being good paper. The ribbon goes last, with a small green flare. Fitch lets the ash fall into the harbour.

"So," says Dunmore. "That is that. I'd have signed it on Thursday if I could have filled the space. I want you to know that, since you were honest with me." He sways, and two of his cutter's men take his weight. "Osric, come to the house tomorrow, not early. Bring your notion about the buoys, and a figure. I find I've an interest in lights on rocks." To you he says, with what is left of his voice, "And you. I still don't know what to call you. I've decided I prefer it."

They carry him up the lane. Fitch lingers one moment on the steps, hat in hand.

"Madam. In Thornby I offered you fifty pounds for what was in that case." He looks at the place where the ash went into the water. "I have never been so glad to be refused."

He follows the others. Nell puts the blanket round your shoulders. From the main quay the cheering is still going on, and the bell.
I sleep until noon. Then I go to the hall and ask Dallow who in Greywater can cut a chart on copper, and how quickly.

You wake to a washed blue sky and a harbour full of the sound of hammers. From the chandlery window you can see the Calloway at anchor inside the bar, with men already aloft clearing the wreck of her topmast, and a boat putting off from her toward the town.

The Guild hall has changed overnight. The long room is crowded with pilots, the same men who were shouting upstairs four days ago, standing three deep in front of Nell's desk where the fair sheet has been pinned up under glass. They are not shouting now. They make way for you without being asked, and one old man with a face like a walnut takes off his cap.

Dallow draws you into the panelled room and shuts the door on them.

"They've been at it since seven. Every one of them has found the place on the sheet where his own father came to grief." He looks as though he has not slept at all, and does not mind. "Copper. There's one hand in this town that can do it, and it's the best north of the capital, though she'd box my ears for saying it. Lise Marrot. She cut the last three Guild charts and the altar plate for the chapel. Her shop's in Cooper's Row, behind the ropewalk."

He hesitates.

"She's slow, I warn you. Not idle, slow. She'll cut nothing she hasn't understood, and she'll ask you why every figure is where it is. Old Pym came out of her shop in tears. A month, I'd have said, for a sheet that size." He scratches his jaw. "The Calloway's master is on his way up here to ask for a copy to take to sea with him. I should like to give him more than a promise. Will you go to her yourself?"
"I'll go now, and I'll take the fair sheet and the sounding ledger. If she wants to know why every figure is where it is, I'm the one who can tell her."

Cooper's Row is a lane of workshops that smells of hot pitch and oak shavings. The engraver's is the last door, under a sign with nothing on it but a burin and a single engraved line, curled like a wave. The window is very clean.

The woman at the bench inside does not look up when the bell rings. She is about forty-five, spare and upright, with cropped iron-grey hair and a leather apron, and she is drawing a steel point through a sheet of copper with her whole forearm, in one long unbroken stroke. A bright thread of metal curls up ahead of the tool. Only when the stroke is finished does she set the burin down, blow the curl away, and turn round on her stool.

"Guild," she says, looking at the roll under your arm. Her accent is not local; the vowels are flatter, from somewhere up the coast. "And not Dallow, nor his clerk. So you're the one the bell was for." She holds out her hands, both, for the sheet. "Unroll it there, on the slab. Don't speak for a minute."

It is a good deal more than a minute. She goes over the chart with a lens, corner to corner, as Corwin Hale went over the compass. She follows the border. She counts the soundings in the channel, moving her lips. She spends a long time on the two leading marks drawn in elevation at the edge.

"The lettering's a clerk's and it's pretty. The line work is yours and it isn't pretty at all. It's correct. I can see where the pen stopped each time to check a figure." She lays the lens down. "Forty-four soundings one way and forty-four back, and three crossings. Why is there a five and a half here, on the north side, in among the sevens?"

"Because that's where the northern edge begins to shelve. It came up yellow sand in the tallow instead of bare rock, on the second run, about two-thirds of the way through. It's the one place a ship could stray and still float, and I want a master to see that it's the forgiving side."

Lise Marrot nods slowly. She picks up a stick of red chalk and makes a tiny tick beside the figure.

"Then it wants a letter by it for the bottom. S for sand. And the sevens want R. If the bottom's the reason, the bottom must be on the plate." She looks up. "You've written it in the ledger. A seaman in a gale doesn't have the ledger. He has what I cut."

She asks eleven more questions. Why the wrecks have names and not only crosses: because the pilots will trust a chart that knows what they know. Why the note about the ebb is so large: because Penhale said so, and he was right. Whether the tower and the beacon will still stand in fifty years: you do not know, and say so, and she writes "beacon to be maintained" in chalk beside the elevation, with a line under it.

At the end she sits back and wipes her fingers on her apron.

"Dallow told you a month. He always tells people a month, to frighten them." There is a gleam in the grey eyes. "A month is for work I have to puzzle out. This, I understand. The line work is spare; there's no shading, no sea monsters, thank God. I can have the channel and the bar on copper in four days, and the lettering in two more, if I do nothing else and you are here to answer when I ask. Not at the hall. Here, on that stool."

She tilts her head at the roll.

"And the title. Your clerk has lettered a ship, a keeper, and two initials. I cut what I'm given. But I've engraved the names of men who did a tenth of this, an inch high. Are you certain?"
"Certain. The cutter and the ledger did the work. Two initials is how I sign everything. Six days, then, and I'll be on that stool every one of them."

"Then I'll cut two initials," says Lise Marrot, "and I'll cut them well."

The six days go by in the smell of copper and lamp oil. She works from first light until the shadows spoil the surface, and you sit on the stool at her elbow with the ledger open, and answer. It is extraordinary to watch. The chart exists on the plate backwards, as in a mirror, and she never once hesitates; the long hook of the bar grows under the burin from north to south, a hair's breadth at a time, and the two fine lines of the channel are each cut in a single stroke, with her breath held.

People come to the door. She sends most of them away. The Calloway's master is let in, a big, quiet man named in the town as Captain Rudd, who stands with his hat in his hands looking at the half-cut plate and says only, "I'll wait for it. I'll not sail without it." Tam comes every afternoon when the Kittiwake is in, and is allowed to sweep up the copper curls. Penhale comes once, at an hour when he believes the shop is empty, and is discovered by both of you standing in front of the title with his cap off. He leaves without a word, very red.

On the sixth evening she inks the plate, wipes it with the heel of her hand, and lays a damp sheet over it. The press is a heavy wooden thing with a star wheel. She leans her weight on the spokes; the bed rumbles through.

She peels the sheet back from one corner and holds it up to the window, right way round at last, black and sharp and wet.

"First proof," she says. "Nobody has seen this but us. Take the lens. Go over every figure against your ledger, and don't be kind. If there's an error it's better found tonight than on a quarterdeck."
I take the lens and the ledger and check every sounding in order, one at a time, with my finger on the ledger line and the lens on the proof.

She lights two lamps and sets them on either side of you, and then, with a tact you would not have expected, goes to the far end of the shop and begins grinding a burin, with her back turned.

The bar is right. The nineteen names are right, and spelled as Tane spelled them. The elevation of the leading marks is exact. You go down the channel sounding by sounding: seven, seven, six and a half, seven. The crossings agree. The letters for the bottom are where they should be, R along the scoured middle, S at the northern edge, M where the river mud begins.

At the thirty-first sounding of the inward run your finger stops on the ledger and the lens stops on the proof, and they do not say the same thing.

The ledger reads five and a half, sand: the shelving place, the forgiving side. On the proof, in the same position, cut with perfect clarity, is a six and a half. It is the only figure on the whole sheet that differs. It makes the edge of the channel look a fathom deeper than it is, at exactly the point where a master would be tempted to stray.

The grinding has stopped. Lise Marrot has turned round on her stool and is watching your face.

"You've found something," she says. "Where?"

I turn the proof and the ledger toward her and put a finger on each. "Thirty-first on the way in. Five and a half in the book, six and a half on the plate. It's the shelving edge, the one I told you about on the first day."

She is across the shop in three strides. She does not look at the proof first; she looks at the ledger, at Tam's five and a half in your pencil, and then at the red chalk tick she made beside it herself six days ago. Then she bends over the copper with the lens.

For a moment she says nothing. A flush climbs slowly up her neck.

"Mine. Entirely mine. A five backwards is very like a six backwards when the light is going, and I cut that corner last thing on Tuesday because I wanted it finished." She straightens up. Her voice is quite calm, and very cold, and none of the coldness is for you. "Twenty-six years, and I put a fathom of water where there's sand, on a chart that's to keep ships off it. If you had been kind tonight, that would have been printed two hundred times."

She takes down a small hammer and a steel punch. Turning the plate over, she finds the spot from behind, sets the punch, and taps: three precise blows. On the face, the six has become a faint smooth bruise in the copper. She burnishes it flat with an agate, leans in, and cuts the five in four strokes.

The second proof comes off the press as the church clock strikes ten. You check the thirty-first sounding before anything else. Five and a half, S.

"Now all of them again," says Lise Marrot. "From the beginning. I've been wrong once tonight, and I don't know that I've only been wrong once." She pulls up a second stool on the other side of the lamp and picks up her own lens. "You read the ledger aloud. I'll read the plate. Start at the Outer Road."
I read every sounding aloud from the ledger, from the nine in the Outer Road to the last five in the mud, and wait at each one for her to answer from the proof.

It takes until midnight. You read, and she answers, figure for figure, in a level voice: "Nine, shell. Seven. Seven. Six and a half, rock." Not one of the others is wrong. At the end she lays down the lens, rubs her eyes with the backs of her wrists, and signs the margin of the proof in pencil with the date and the word "passed."

"You sign it too," she says. "Initials will do. I want it written down that two people read it."

She prints through the next day and the next. By Saturday there are two hundred sheets drying on lines across the shop like washing, and the Guild's seal has been pressed into the corner of each. Dallow sets the price himself, in front of the pilots: one shilling, to any master, of any port.

The first copies are sold from Nell's desk on Monday morning. The queue runs out of the front door and along the quay. Captain Rudd is at the head of it, and pays with a guinea and will not take the change. Behind him are fishermen, coasting skippers, a Dutchman, and, some way back, waiting his turn like anyone else with both hands wrapped in clean linen, a slight grey-haired man in a plain coat.

When he reaches the desk, Nell looks up and loses her place in the ledger.

"One, if you please," says Dunmore. Fitch, beside him, puts a shilling on the wood, since his employer cannot yet manage coins. Dunmore's eyes go to the corner of the sheet as Nell rolls it: the cutter, the keeper, the two small letters. He reads them. He looks across the room to where you are standing by the pigeonholes, and inclines his head, and says nothing whatever about them.

"I'm told," he remarks instead, to nobody in particular, "that the Guild is to advertise for a keeper of buoys. I thought I'd ask what the post pays."
I come over to the desk. "A penny a ton on every keel, Mr Dunmore, and three tenders to maintain. Master Dallow has the figures. How are the hands?"

"Mending. Your honey answers very well; my housekeeper is astonished, and has taken the credit." He holds them up, two neat white parcels. "The surgeon says I'll have the use of them by the spring, and scars across both palms to remember a quarter of a minute by. I find I don't object."

Dallow has come down the stairs at the sound of the voice. The two men look at each other across the crowded room: the heavy, rolling pilot and the slight shipowner, who have been on opposite sides of every question in Greywater for twenty years.

"A penny a ton," says Dallow. "Paid quarterly. The tenders to be painted any colour the keeper likes."

"Black," says Dunmore, "with a yellow stripe. My men are used to it." The room, which has gone silent, lets out its breath in something like a laugh. He takes the rolled chart under his arm, awkwardly, and turns to go. At the door he stops beside you.

"A carrier told me this morning that you have asked about the road east," he says, low enough that only you can hear. "Inland. I shan't ask where. I've lost the habit of asking where you are going, and I mean to keep it lost." He glances at the brass case on your back. "But the Guild will want its surveyor for the river above the town, and the two estuaries north of this one, and I daresay Osric is working himself up to offer it. I hope you'll hear him before you decide. This coast has been drowning people for three hundred years. It took you a fortnight to stop it in one place."

He bows, and goes out into the sunlight. Dallow is making his way toward you through the pilots, clearing his throat, with a folded paper in his hand that is not a writ.
"Before you offer me anything, Osric, tell me what it is and what it would keep me from. I have a promise to keep on the road south before the winter."

Dallow stops, the paper half unfolded, and gives a rueful grunt.

"Am I as plain as that? Nell said I was." He steers you by the elbow to the window seat, out of the crowd. "Here it is, then, with nothing dressed up. The Guild wants a standing surveyor. It never had one; it had pilots who drew, and you've seen what that got us. There's the river from here to the weir, which silts. There's Marrow estuary, and the Sands beyond it, which have killed as many as our bar. Three years' work, maybe four."

He opens the paper flat on his knee. It is in Nell's hand, with a figure in it that makes the fee for the bar look like pocket money.

"A hundred and twenty pounds a year. The use of the Kittiwake and her people from April to October. A room in the hall for your instruments, with a north light. And a seat at the pilots' table, which no one not born in this town has ever had." He clears his throat again. "What it would keep you from is anything else, for three years. I'll not pretend otherwise. And I'd need something to write at the top of the articles. The agent's letter did well enough for one chart. It won't do for a seat at the table."

He folds his hands over the paper and looks at you with those pale, creased, patient eyes.

"I don't want an answer today. I want you to go south, keep your promise, and think. The articles will lie in the strongroom till the first of April. Is that fair?"
"It's fair, and it's more than I expected. Keep the articles until April. If I come back, I'll come by the harbor road, and I'll give you what to write at the top of them myself."

"Then I'll have Nell leave the line blank," says Dallow. "She's good at blanks. She left one for a month and it turned out to be you."

He shakes your hand in both of his, and then, being a man who dislikes having been moved in public, goes off at once to shout at somebody about mooring fees.

The fee for the bar is paid that afternoon, in gold, counted out on Nell's desk and signed for with two letters. Nell watches you make them.

"I've been trying to guess for a fortnight," she confesses. "I had it as Eliza for a while. Then Maud." She blots the receipt. "I shan't ask. I've a list of eleven and I'd rather keep them all than lose ten." She comes round the desk and embraces you quickly and hard, leaving a smudge of ink on your collar.

Your last evening is at the widow's table. She has roasted a fowl, which Tam says she has not done since her husband's funeral. Penhale is there, in a clean jersey, and Hob, who has been sober and silent for two weeks and looks five years older for it.
